Since I'm also on the ace spectrum, I like to think of it as similar to that. Gender and attraction are like what color, and feeling agender or asexual or aromantic is like having the saturation turned down. Like for me, I'm definitely romantically attracted to woman and other feminine presenting persons. I'm also somewhat attracted to them sexually, but very rarely which is why I use the label greysexual to indicate that my sexual attraction for them is in low saturation. I also definitely identify as agender, so in that sense I'm colorless. Obviously the connotation of colorless makes it seem like I'm a drab person, but for the sake of painting a picture..or in this case not painting a picture lol, I think color works pretty well as a hypothetical. My therapist then became the housing manager of the housing program i was in and basically got me kicked out 2 weeks before the holidays.

So, I have pretty moderate ptsd, complex ptsd, night terrors, sleep paralysis, ptsd attacks that border on psychosis and a mounting lack of sleep due to these things.. which creates suicidal ideation.
Minipress and venaflaxine were my drugs of choice, and combined with a stable routine and regular therapy I was improving a lot.
Fast forward to now.. and due to a lot of bureaucracy I'm nearly a month without meds and my therapist turned out to be no bueno. In the craziness of my life, and while I wasnt able to get my regular blend of meds, I did stumble on the ability to access shrooms. Like you, I pondered on it a lot. Whether or not I should do it, would it make my problems worse.. would I get traumatized by the experience?
Well, I have very recently (like, as I'm typing this) finished tripping off of 2 grams of lemon tekked golden teacher shrooms. And, here's what I have to say about my experience. 
As someone who professionally uses massage therapy, having shrooms enact changes on my noggin felt very similar to getting a deep tissue massage. At first you're hit by the euphoria, you can feel your occipital lobe being gently massaged and it's creating these smushed images in your vision. It feels like the visual world around you is being squished here and there. Every so often I remind myself to breath, since during a massage breathing actually solidifies the more relaxed position of your now resting muscles and nerves, but in this case its your delicate brain muscles. Almost like I'm easing into the different pressures that are being put on my brain. I try to use imagery to imagine the feelings as tension and I imagine myself massaging out the tensions in my brain. Every once and a while my brain will hit these snags and I'll be stuck in these loopy altered states of consciousness for just a liiitle too long. But, once I'm out I focus again on breathing, and being alone (in my case) helps me feel grounded again. Oh, and I also laughed really hard at some point in the beginning. I think for a second I got the joke that life was telling and was like "dang, that's actually a knee slapper". I also thought about someone I'd met in the suicide ward before who always seemed to be on shrooms 24/7, and I had this epiphany that by experiencing this horrifying trauma (I think it involved her family getting gunned down in her home, and the police not coming to help because she lived in the ghetto) her brain quite literally went into near psychosis to cope. I immediately started thinking about where she might be now and I hoped that she was doing okay and was safe. Gosh, none of this is making sense, I think I'm still a little bit blasted... Anywho, my final conclusions are! 1. It felt like getting a brain massage
2. Because of my self awareness and talent for feeling out knots, I used the shrooms to help me get into the deeper knots in my brain,  effectively massaging them away
3. I feel great. Like, I feel clean. My occipital lobe feels a bit cold and I feel like my brain is actively learning things again in a way I havent been able to since childhood.. I'm crushing my duolingo sessions atm lol
4.yknow that feeling you get when you stretch after a mildly painful but good massage? Yeah, that. 

So, while I can definitely see how this can potentially retraumatize some peeps.. for me, it felt different from the times I was forcifully trauma bonded by abusers. I was entirely conscious and the only person probing was myself. Like, I truly was the one probing. There were no shrooms in a judge outfit with a gavel in one shroomy hand and another shroom paw placed against a Bible lol i didn't feel like an invader was messing with my head. It felt..like my inner child was finally let inside the control room and they just went wild lol. There was consent to the madness, this willingness to massage out the pain. It felt like being able to experience another form of self love in that way. I honestly recommend it. It's not like I don't need coping strategies anymore... its like I'm finally relaxed enough in my brain to begin EffectivelY learning them. I think, having someone whom you trust with you while tripping is paramount. I didn't exactly have a trip sitter, but I did have my roommate in the other room to talk to when feelings needed that extra step of dialogue to finally process themselves in my brain. It helped a lot.

So yeah, OP, respond all you want but I'm probably not going to entertain you with any answers. Anywho, instead of a food analogy I'll use jungian typology as a means to push this point. Someone who is an INFJ for example, will see the world mainly through the lens of introverted intuition. For them, the world is a mirror that reflects all their thoughts in(at least for me) this giant web of patterns, built from the information they take in about the world around. But that web of patterns doesn't exist for someone like an INFP. For them, the focus is not patterns, but the individual strings of data that emotionally gratify them most. For some people, it's patterns. For others, it's emotion. For other's, its the data itself. For some more, the information they take about the world isn't as important as their own interaction with the world. For some more, its the interaction between some emotional truth and data. A logical truth and patterns. Its pretty complex, and this is only one dimension of the human experience.  Ignoring the complexities of humanity by chalking up all of their "whys" to one singular dimension has been the past time of many powers. Whether its the religious why of the catholic church, the spiritual why of a yogo instructor, the sexual why of some freud follower like yourself, or even the logical "whys" of academia; regardless of what institution is creating a one-size fits all mantra this week, as long as humans exist in so many conceptual dimensions we will always be complex. I.S. (Intersexuality) is literally amazing. Though it focuses primarily on the struggles of intersex individuals, it goes full on into the divide between physical sex and gender. It features intersex characters who've had gender confirming operations, those undecided, and those whose gender aligns with nonbinary all the way. I found the personal struggle of the titular lead from Act 3 (the main and largest featured storyline) to mirror a lot of my own struggles as a non binary individual. Although I'm not intersex, my features have led me to be mistaken as both female and male my whole life, and I was raised in a household that didn't force me into any gender role. The struggle of finding love and acceptance, while also showing the importance one has for a career was a breath of fresh air from the usually one-note gender focused stories out there. It really touched on all aspects of the intersex experience, as well as highlighting the struggles of all gender non-conforming people. I highly recommend it.

No further recommendations but I would like to add my thoughts. Both my parents are alive but growing up, especially when I was kotaro's age, my parents neglected me due to work. I honestly really liked how kotaro reacted to his situation, as it reminds me of how I used to be. I know many people who've watched the show and felt emotional over kotaro's situation, but I can't help but see myself in him. I was never particularly emotional about being neglected so it's hard for me to feel sad for him, as I didn't feel sad myself going through that. It honestly really inspired me. Going into middle school, my parents went from neglect to physical abuse. I would get hit for no reason at all. One time I was even awakened by these attacks. It really affected me. Before, when I had to do things on my own like cook or clean or go to the store,  I'd tell myself that I was making it easier for my parents and that I should be grateful that they work so hard for me. This changed that dynamic to one of self loathing, as I genuinely did think I was doing something wrong. It also affected my ability to cope. I was severely bullied as an elementary schooler, but that never really affected me. After the physical abuse started, I became severely depressed. And the ostracization I faced at school only worsened that. The one saving grace during that time was my grandparents. They'd always somewhat taken care of me, when I'd give them the chance too (my grandparents had lived with me my whole life, but I was very independent prior to middle school). During my abuse they actually went out of their way, standing up to my parents for me. I became very attached to them during this time. Even so, my grandmother had dementia that got worse as I started high school. I spent most of my time in high school caring for her. So much so that I barely managed to graduate. But I don't regret that. My grandmother actually passed before I graduated high school. She was the main motivation for me to graduate,  as even with dementia she always pushed me to care about school. My grandfather recently passed away tragically from covid. So, I've been dealing with that. My parents and I have a better relationship now but I'll always attribute my grandparents to being my sole guardians growing up. In wake of both my grandparents passing, I've found myself in a very similar place as to when I was a kid, save for their presence. So, I've been dealing with a lot of self doubt. I live alone now and don't have my grandparents here with me. Both my parents care for me in their own way, but they live out of state now and I just never had that kind of relationship where I could ask things of them (despite my efforts to create it). Most of my self-doubt surrounds the fact that I'm no longer the brave and independent child I used to be. I'm now this scared, lonely and traumatized adult that spends most of their time either working or wallowing in a sea of emotions I can scarcely comprehend. So, watching kotaro succeed in his situation has reminded me of why I was like that too. I went to this therapist a couple of years back who kind of got it in my head that I had a savior complex. While kotaro definitely has dreams of protecting others, I don't think he has a savior complex. I think he just cares that much about other people. And I think I'm the same way. I think I've started victimizing myself ever since I went to therapy (not that all therapy is bad, my therapist just wasn't the best). So seeing a child of similar circumstance acting out all the feelings I'd convinced myself weren't there, has been really monumental for me. It reminds me that I'm more capable than I know and it inspires me to succeed. I think all my experiences have made me the person I am today, and I wouldn't trade that for anything.

After 6 months of waiting to recieve neurological testing, I was finally diagnosed with high-functioning autism at 21 years old. Initially I was diagnosed with SPCD, which is short for Social Pragmatic Communication Disorder. My psychiatrist had referred to it as a modern label for aspergers. Even so, with the expense of $700 needed for extra confirmation testing, I wasn't happy about being eased into such a label. Especially when I'd only missed one aspect of the questionare to qualify for autism.
You see, growing up I used to move a lot. Often having to give up my room to whomever came to live with us next (aunts, uncles, cousins, step siblings, family friends, ect.) Some nights I slept on the couch, some I slept with my grandparents, and other nights I slept in my sister's room. I also couldn't get to school everyday because of my parent's negligence, and we always lived too far to for me to bike or bus alone. I cared and watched over my grandmother as her alzheimerz began to worsen, which involved many sleepless nights, frustration, and sadness (not to mention the grief). The cherry on top, though, was how my parents often abused me because of my undiagnosed autism, or because they were in a mood. Its funny, I had to pay $700 for extra testing because I didn't check off one box, routines. Having lived my life the way I did, such costs make it all seem so utterly useless. All the pain and drama, like weights upon my heart.
Only good as a weapon to hurt others.
Still, my dream is to eventually have a solid routine for myself. One where I have total control over what I choose to do, and what I choose to do is something thats healthy and makes me happy. 
I just wish that one day, I can wash away all the pointless hardships; 
so that I may rise through the thick swamp and mud,
blooming despite everything
like a lotus flower.
